summary.text: Actaeon the Theban hunter, grandson of Cadmus, wandered into the vale of Gargaphie and saw Diana bathing — and the goddess flung water on his face, set antlers on his brow, and drove him as a stag until his own fifty hounds, blind to their master, ran him down and tore him apart on Cithaeron.

chapters.title: The sacred pool
chapters.text: When the day was spent, Actaeon of Hyantis called off the hunt and sent his comrades home; but he wandered alone into woods he did not know and came to Gargaphie, where Diana bathed with her nymphs in a grotto of cool stone and a pool edged with grass. Apollodorus says Chiron bred him to the chase, and records three charges against him without choosing one: that Zeus was angry because he wooed Semele; that he saw Artemis bathing; or that he boasted himself the better hunter.

chapters.title: The stag
chapters.text: The nymphs shrieked; Diana stood taller than her guards and wished for her arrows, but had only the spring. She dashed water on Actaeon's face and cursed him to tell the tale if he could: horns sprang from his head, his neck lengthened, his hands became hooves, and dappled hide covered the hunter who had been the grandson of Cadmus. He fled in terror, marveling at his speed, and saw his antlers in a stream.

chapters.title: The hounds
chapters.text: Ashamed to go home, afraid to trust the woods, Actaeon hesitated — until his own pack found him. Blackfoot and Tracer gave the signal; the Arcadian and Spartan dogs followed, and the whole pack fixed their jaws in the flesh of their master, who could only groan in a stag's voice and turn entreating eyes on teeth that did not know him. His friends called Actaeon! Actaeon! while he died; Diana's wrath, Ovid says, did not abate until the torn flesh ceased to live.
